opening.headline: Two patterns—orchestrator-worker and evaluator-improver—are used when you cannot anticipate downstream tasks or need to repeatedly improve output quality.
body: When asked to fix this bug, it's not possible in advance to know how many files need to be modified. Even if the fix is chained together, the required steps vary depending on the input. In some cases, the initial result falls short of the target quality, and improvement becomes possible with further refinement.

In this course, we examine orchestrators and workers that dynamically divide work from the central authority, as well as evaluators and improvers that iteratively generate and assess to enhance quality. Since repetition carries the risk of infinite loops, we also discuss how to set termination conditions and cost bounds.
As of 2026-10: gemini-2.5-flash in the example is provided primarily for existing users. In a new project, check and replace the currently accessible model ID and run the example.

items.prompt: How many files need to be changed? (Number of child operations)
items.answer: At the time a request is received, it is not possible to know exactly which files need to be modified. Since subtasks vary depending on the input, fixed chains cannot predefine the steps. In such cases, the orchestrator-worker pattern is used.

items.prompt: When does it become sufficiently good? (The point at which quality is achieved)
items.answer: It's common for initial results to fall short of the desired objectives. Iteratively refining based on evaluation can improve outcomes. The pattern used in such scenarios is known as the evaluator-improver cycle, and it's difficult to determine in advance how many iterations will be sufficient.

items.prompt: What is the problem when trying to unlock both of them together?
items.answer: Allowing work to increase and repeatedly striving to improve quality leads to more calls and the risk of infinite looping. Therefore, this class addresses two questions: how to handle work that dynamically increases, and when to stop continuous improvement.

screens.outro: Let us reflect on your experiences with the question in mind.

screens.title: View when work dynamically increases
screens.lead: After first thinking through the question mentally and making a choice, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Answers are not entered or submitted.

items.prompt: How do you handle scenarios where the workload dynamically increases?
items.answer: If it's not possible to define all steps from the beginning, it's necessary to establish plans midway and divide tasks among team members. In a human team, the team leader receives requests, breaks down the work, assigns it to individual responsible parties, and then aggregates the results. The orchestrator-worker model follows this structure.

items.prompt: Was there ever a case where the initially planned number of stages was maintained until the end?
items.answer: It is generally not sustainable. As investigations or modification tasks proceed, the number of items requiring verification continually increases. Therefore, designs that fix the number of stages are prone to breaking, and a structure capable of accommodating growing workloads is required.

items.prompt: Have you reviewed the results again and experienced any improvement?
items.answer: Showing an initial draft to a colleague to receive feedback and make revisions usually improves the outcome. However, once the same feedback starts repeating, further revisions will not lead to improvement. Determining when repetition of feedback becomes worthwhile is key when involving evaluators and improvers.

screens.outro: First, let's look at the structure of dividing work at the central level.

screens.title: Orchestrator-Worker: The center splits, assigns, and merges.
screens.lead: Follow the flow step by step from request to result combination. Select the right arrow to view the next step.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the structure where the central orchestrator divides requests into subtasks and delegates them to workers, then synthesizes the results.

steps.title: 1. The request arrives at the central node.
steps.body: The request first goes to the orchestrator, the central LLM. The orchestrator takes on the role of determining what actions need to be taken, rather than performing the tasks directly. At this stage, the list of subordinate tasks has not yet been determined.

steps.title: 2. Dynamically decomposes
steps.body: The orchestrator dynamically breaks down work based on input. For coding tasks, the number of files to modify and the specific changes required per file vary depending on the task. While parallelization and orchestration are similar, the key difference lies in the fact that subordinate tasks are not predefined in advance and are instead determined by the input by the orchestrator—this is what enables the pattern's flexibility.

steps.title: 3. Delegates to the worker
steps.body: The decomposed subtasks are delegated to the worker LLM. The worker performs only the subtasks assigned to it. The number of workers varies depending on the number of subtasks.

steps.title: 4. Collects and synthesizes the results
steps.body: The orchestrator aggregates the results returned by the workers into a single result. Since the aggregation side is central, the orchestrator is ultimately responsible for the final result. Additionally, it may spawn further subtasks during the aggregation process if needed.

steps.title: 5. Suitable duties
steps.body: Anthropic provides examples such as coding products that repeatedly modify complex files and search tasks that gather and analyze information from multiple sources. In both cases, the input determines what to find and how to modify.

steps.title: 6. Two forms of ownership with the same structure
steps.body: OpenAI's documentation states that in a multi-agent workflow, determining who takes responsibility for the final user response is the first design choice. There are two approaches: one where an expert receives the response, and another where a manager holds onto the response and calls experts like tools. The orchestrator-worker model is closer to the latter approach.

screens.outro: Now we will look at the evaluators-improvers and their termination mechanism repeatedly improving quality.

screens.title: Evaluator-Improver and Termination Conditions
screens.lead: This is an example of representing the evaluator-improver loop using LoopAgent from ADK. Select the comments next to the code to verify which line handles iteration and termination.

visual.alt: A diagram showing a loop where the author creates a draft, the reviewer provides feedback, and the author revises, ending with a termination condition.
labels: A signal that the evaluator is sufficient
Token and call counts increase with each iteration (cost cap required)

data.code:
from google.adk.agents import LoopAgent, LlmAgent
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

def exit_loop(tool_context: ToolContext):
    """Calls only when it is said there is nothing more to fix in the critique."""
    tool_context.actions.escalate = True
    return {}

writer = LlmAgent(name="WriterAgent", model="gemini-2.5-flash",
                  instruction="Writes a draft or revises it based on criticism.")
critic = LlmAgent(name="CriticAgent", model="gemini-2.5-flash",
                  instruction="Critique the draft. If no issues are found, call exit_loop.",
                  tools=[exit_loop])

refine_loop = LoopAgent(
    name="RefinementLoop",
    sub_agents=[writer, critic],
    max_iterations=5,
)

notes.note: LoopAgent is a template workflow that repeatedly executes subordinate agents until a specified number of iterations or a termination condition is met. The execution is managed deterministically by the agent itself, not by an AI model.

This is a tool that generates termination signals. When "escalate" is enabled, the loop ends. If this device is absent and no maximum count is specified, LoopAgent will not define when to stop and may run infinitely.
Agent for writing the role of contributor. Initially drafts a first version, and then in subsequent rounds refines it by incorporating feedback.
An agent for critiquing the evaluator's role. Clear evaluation criteria ensure useful feedback, and if no issues are found, it calls exit_loop to send a termination signal.
Iterates over writer and critic in sequence. max_iterations is the simplest cost ceiling, and here it is set to a maximum of five times. If a signal comes first, it stops before that.

screens.outro: Two termination devices were visible. Let's follow along with how they are used in the example.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Review-Edit Iteration of the Code Modification Agent
screens.lead: The instructor explains three rounds in which the code modification agent receives a review and fixes a patch. Select the right arrow to proceed through the rounds.

steps.title: Case Setup
steps.body: The agent modifies the bug fix patch, and the reviewer evaluates the test failure reasons and code quality. The evaluation criteria are as clear as test pass/fail outcomes. This is a well-matched scenario between evaluator and improver—where evaluation criteria are explicit and the value of repetition can be measured.

steps.title: Round 1
steps.body: When the revision agent creates a draft patch, the review agent identifies two types of issues: one is the omission of boundary value handling, and the other is a violation of test name conventions. The number of identified issues at this stage is two.

steps.title: Round 2
steps.body: The fixes have addressed the boundary value issues and reduced the number of intelligent checks by one. With fewer intelligent checks, the improvements are now clearly visible. This section involves iterative value generation, and the accumulated cost increases by the number of rounds.

steps.title: Round 3
steps.body: The reviewer repeats the same critique. Even after revisions, the same criticism remains, indicating that improvements have stalled. Further iteration here only accumulates costs without yielding better results.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The flow of three rounds follows a pattern where the number of insights decreases from two to one, then repeats with the same insight. The point at which the insight count does not decrease serves as the criterion to halt repetition. This criterion must be explicitly defined as a termination condition in the code. When a human reviews the process, they also follow a similar principle—when the same insight is exchanged three times, they change their approach or request input from another person. By recording the number of insights per round, this judgment can be made numerically rather than intuitively.

screens.outro: We will now proceed to examine how specific numerical values are determined for termination conditions and cost limits.

data.notes: The device in the table is not used singly but stacked. The review pass declaration follows the normal termination path, while the remaining three devices serve as safety mechanisms in case the normal path fails. It is important not to hide failure cases when safety mechanisms activate, but instead to pass the results to humans for verification. The upper limit of three retries is justified by the fact that additional repetitions beyond three times offer little cost-benefit. By specifying both a maximum number of attempts and an evaluator's termination signal—as demonstrated in the ADK document—when the signal arrives first, the process ends early; if the signal does not arrive, it still stops at the upper limit. Frequent reaching of the upper limit signals a problem with the evaluation criteria or the guidance of the correction agent, so it is essential to investigate the root cause before increasing the number of retries. Setting a cost upper limit using both call count and token volume as axes is safe. Stop when either axis is first reached.

screens.outro: We will conclude by grouping the two patterns and the stop mechanism under one reference.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Dynamic tasks and loops require a termination mechanism.
screens.lead: We combine and organize the decision criteria for both patterns along with the safety mechanisms placed on repetition.

paragraphs: When the breakdown of subtasks cannot be known in advance, use an orchestrator-worker architecture. The central LLM observes the input and divides the work among workers, who then produce results that are synthesized centrally. Similar to parallelization, but differs in that subtasks are not pre-defined—they are determined dynamically based on the input, such as how many files need to be modified or how many sources need to be searched.

When quality needs to be iteratively improved, identify evaluators and improvers. This pattern is effective under two conditions: first, when feedback from humans results in clearly improved responses, and second, when LLMs can also provide such feedback. The evaluation criteria must be clear and capable of measuring the value of iteration. If the criteria are vague, evaluators' judgments become unstable, and iteration fails to lead to improvement.

Iteration must include both a termination condition and a cost cap. Since each iteration incurs additional calls and tokens, without a cap costs would grow indefinitely. A safe approach is to combine a signal indicating sufficient evaluator feedback with a maximum number of iterations; when the same issue is repeated, improvement has stalled and iteration should stop. When the cost cap is reached, an exit path should be predefined to hand over the current best result and unresolved issues to a human. Finally, before adopting these two patterns, first verify whether a simpler structure—such as a single call or a fixed chain—is sufficient. If the problem can be resolved with a single call or a fixed sequence, neither an orchestrator nor iteration is necessary.

In summary, the decision-making order consists of three questions: Can we predefine the subtasks? Is there a clear criterion to evaluate the quality of the results? Do we have a mechanism to halt repetition? The first two questions determine what pattern to use, while the third question establishes whether that pattern can be used safely. If we cannot answer all three questions, it means the structure has not yet been ready for use. Simply going through this check once during the design phase is sufficient to largely prevent endless loops.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The two patterns are not mutually exclusive. The orchestrator may apply an evaluator-improver iteration to each of the subtasks it divides, but it must also be more careful in setting cost upper bounds accordingly. Designing an iteration means designing when to stop. The point at which improvement ceases becomes the criterion for determining the number of iterations.

glossary.def: This is a pattern where the central LLM dynamically divides work and delegates it to worker LLMs, then combines the results.
This is a pattern where one call generates a response and another call provides evaluation and feedback, repeatedly improving quality.
Rules for terminating a loop. The maximum number of iterations and a signal indicating sufficient evaluation are typical examples.
This is due to the growing number of recursive calls and the budget limits imposed on tokens.

misconceptions.fact: The structure is similar, but parallelization involves pre-defined subtasks. The orchestrator-worker determines the subtasks based on the input, with the central LLM specifying these subtasks.

misconceptions.myth: The more it is repeated, the better the results become.
misconceptions.fact: If the same issue repeats, improvement has stopped. Therefore, termination conditions and cost limits are necessary.

misconceptions.myth: The loop is stopped by the framework itself.
misconceptions.fact: LoopAgent does not specify when to stop on its own. Maximum iteration count or termination signals must be designed directly.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Subtasks whose exact details cannot be known in advance are dynamically divided by the orchestrator.
Performance evaluation is effective when the criteria are clear and improvement is measurable.
Iteration must have both a termination condition and a cost limit.
The point at which improvement stops serves as the criterion for determining the number of iterations.
